lesson.title: The Meiotic Mistake Behind Extra and Missing Chromosomes
lesson.summary: Nondisjunction is the failure of chromosomes to separate properly during meiosis, and depending on whether it happens in meiosis I or meiosis II, it produces gametes with an extra or missing chromosome in predictable patterns.
lesson.body:
Meiosis depends on two carefully choreographed separation events. In meiosis I, homologous chromosomes, each still made of two sister chromatids, are pulled apart to opposite poles. In meiosis II, which resembles a normal mitotic division, the sister chromatids of each chromosome are finally separated from each other. Both steps rely on the spindle apparatus correctly attaching to and pulling apart chromosomes at anaphase. Nondisjunction is what happens when that separation fails: instead of splitting apart, a pair of chromosomes or a pair of sister chromatids moves together to the same pole.

The consequences depend on which division goes wrong. If nondisjunction occurs in meiosis I, an entire pair of homologous chromosomes fails to separate and both homologs end up in the same secondary cell. Meiosis II then proceeds normally for that cell, splitting the sister chromatids of each homolog apart, so the end result is two gametes carrying two copies of that chromosome and two gametes carrying zero copies. Starting from one primary cell that undergoes meiosis I nondisjunction for a given chromosome, all four resulting gametes end up abnormal: two with an extra copy and two with none.

If nondisjunction instead occurs in meiosis II, meiosis I has already separated the homologous chromosomes correctly, so one secondary cell has already received the normal single copy of that chromosome, present as two sister chromatids. If those sister chromatids then fail to separate in meiosis II, that one secondary cell produces one gamete with two copies of the chromosome and one gamete with zero copies. The other secondary cell, unaffected by the error, divides normally and produces two gametes each with the normal single copy. So starting from the same primary cell, meiosis II nondisjunction produces two normal gametes, one gamete with an extra copy, and one gamete with a missing copy, a milder outcome than meiosis I nondisjunction in terms of the fraction of abnormal gametes.

Either way, fertilization of an abnormal gamete by a normal gamete from the other parent produces a zygote with the wrong total number of copies of that chromosome, since a normal gamete always contributes exactly one copy. A gamete with an extra copy, fertilized normally, yields a zygote with three copies of that chromosome instead of two. A gamete missing a copy yields a zygote with only one copy. This abnormal chromosome number in the resulting individual is called aneuploidy, which the next chapter examines in detail, including why some of these outcomes are compatible with life and others are not.
